title: "Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap"
subtitle: "Why one great defensive lineman lives in the backfield and another never moves, and how both of them win"
description: "The technique numbers from the defense's side of the ball: the nose, the 3-technique, the 4i and 5-technique, the 9 and the wide-9, and the body each spot asks for; one-gap (attack and penetrate) versus two-gap (control, read, shed) play and what each trades away; how a defensive lineman fights a down block, a reach block and a double team; setting the edge and contain; and line movement, the slant and the angle."
glossary:
  One-gap: "A style of defensive line play in which each lineman is responsible for a single gap: he lines up in or shaded toward it, attacks it at the snap, and leaves the other gaps to his teammates."
  Two-gap: "A style of defensive line play in which a lineman lines up head-up on a blocker, controls him with his hands, reads where the ball is going, and then sheds the block to fill the gap on whichever side the ball comes, so one defender covers two gaps."
  Penetration: "A defender getting across the line of scrimmage and into the offense's backfield fast, through a gap, to disrupt a play before it develops; the aim of one-gap line play."
  Wide-9: "An alignment for a defensive end far outside the offensive tackle: one to two or more yards outside the tight end, or, with no tight end, just as far beyond where one would stand (roughly three to four yards outside the tackle), usually in a sprinter's stance (a three-point stance with the weight forward and tilted toward the quarterback). A 9 sits on the tight end's outside shoulder; the wide-9 is a clear step or two beyond. It gives the end the widest angle to rush the passer at the cost of a wider running lane inside him."
  "Set the edge": "The job of the outermost defender at the line on a run toward him: take on the blocker at or near the line of scrimmage with his outside arm free, so the run cannot get outside him and the ball carrier has to turn back inside toward teammates."
  Contain: "A defender's rule to keep the ball carrier, especially a quarterback on a scramble, bootleg or keeper, from getting outside him; for edge rushers on a pass, not rushing past the quarterback's depth and opening an escape lane."
  "Slant (line movement)": "A called line movement in which defensive linemen step hard across the face of the blocker in front of them at the snap, into the next gap over, gaining only a little ground, usually all in the same direction, while the linebackers shift the other way to fill the gaps the line left."
  "Angle (line movement)": "A called movement in which a defensive lineman steps at about 45 degrees into the gap beside him at the snap, moving over one gap while still getting upfield; a shorter, more penetrating move than a slant, often by one or two linemen rather than the whole line."

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"}
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, Rectangle, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style
from gridiron.play import draw_marker

GREEN = "#0f7a55"         # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]  # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
OL_KEYS = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(labels="full"):
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled LT..RT ("full") or with one letter, T G C G T ("short")."""
    short = {"LT": "T", "LG": "G", "C": "C", "RG": "G", "RT": "T"}
    return [p.moved(label=(p.key if labels == "full" else short[p.key])) for p in offense("singleback")
            if p.key in OL_KEYS]


def te(side=1, key=None, label=None):
    """An in-line tight end: Y on the right, U on the left."""
    key = key or ("Y" if side > 0 else "U")
    return O(key, "TE", -0.7, side * 4.8, label or key)


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def gap_tag(fld, p, d, w, text, color=GREEN, fontsize=8.5):
    """A gap letter in a small rounded box."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight="bold", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=1.0))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=10):
    """Mark a point (a tackle, a meeting point) with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)


def lane(fld, p, w0, w1, d0, d1, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """Shade a rectangular lane (a run lane, a gap) from width w0 to w1 and depth d0 to d1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=0.9, ls=ls, zorder=0.8))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, lw=1.5, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'what if' or 'intent' path through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    if end == "arrow":   # dashed all the way to a short solid head on the last 25% of the last leg
        xs, ys = np.asarray(xs, float), np.asarray(ys, float)
        hx, hy = xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])
        xs = np.concatenate([xs[:-1], [hx, xs[-1]]]); ys = np.concatenate([ys[:-1], [hy, ys[-1]]])
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1] if end == "arrow" else xs, ys[:-1] if end == "arrow" else ys, color=color, lw=lw,
                ls=dash, zorder=6)
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))


def bracket(fld, p, d, w0, w1, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2, stem_to=None):
    """A bar spanning the gaps a two-gapper owns, with end ticks and an optional stem to the player."""
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=5)
    for w in (w0, w1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d - 0.35, w), _P(fld, p, d + 0.35, w)
        fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5)
    if stem_to is not None:
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d, (w0 + w1) / 2), _P(fld, p, *stem_to)
        fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=4.5)


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:   # yard numbers, not technique labels
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def front(spec, lbs=(), others=()):
    """Defensive linemen from (key, technique, side) triples, labelled with their technique number,
    plus (key, d, w, label) linebackers and any other defenders."""
    out = [D(k, "DL", 1.0, T(t, s), t) for k, t, s in spec]
    out += [D(k, "LB", d, w, lab) for k, d, w, lab in lbs]
    out += [D(k, "S", d, w, lab) for k, d, w, lab in others]
    return out


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for the simulated plays --------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), enter=(), ring_r=0.85):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    snap = df[df["frameId"] == int((tmap - 0.0).abs().idxmin())]
    first = snap[snap["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                 & snap["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]       # players whose marker fits whole at the snap ...
    ids = set(first["_id"]) | {"football"}
    inside = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1]) & cur["y"].between(ylo, yhi)]
    ids |= set(inside["_id"]) & set(enter)                         # players allowed to walk into the picture
    shown = cur[cur["_id"].isin(ids) | (cur["side"] == "ball")]    # ... stay in every frame (clipped at the edge)
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), ring_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    for patch in ax.patches:
        patch.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2, after=None, enter=()):
    """Numbered frame strip. `moments` is a list of (play, t, tag): several plays may share one strip,
    which is how a branching play (same start, two endings) is shown in print."""
    cache = {}
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(moments) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.62 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(moments):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, (play, t, tag)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, moments)):
        if id(play) not in cache:
            cache[id(play)] = tracking(play)
        fld = panel(ax, play, cache[id(play)], t, lateral, window, rings, enter)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, i)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.2f} s".replace("0 s", " s")
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}" + (f"   {tag}" if tag else ""), fontsize=8.3, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.1, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(segments, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=4.6, after=None, enter=()):
    """Web version: each (play, tag, [(t, note), ...]) segment played in turn, notes as captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.45))
    frames = []
    for play, tag, notes in segments:
        df = tracking(play)
        tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
        frames += [(play, df, float(tmap[f]), tag, notes) for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique())]

    def update(k):
        play, df, t, tag, notes = frames[k]
        ax.clear()
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, enter)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, -1)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (f"  {tag}" if tag else "")
        cur = [n for tt, n in notes if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(txt + (("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""), fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK,
                     loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=range(len(frames)), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(moments, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), after=None, enter=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=notes, rings=rings, ncols=ncols, width_in=width_in,
              after=after, enter=enter)
        plt.show()
        return
    segs = []
    for play, t, tag in moments:
        if not segs or segs[-1][0] is not play:
            segs.append((play, tag, []))
    for (play, t, tag), n in zip(moments, notes):
        for s in segs:
            if s[0] is play:
                s[2].append((t, n))
    if len(segs) > 1:   # later branches share the opening frames: show the first branch's opening notes too
        opening = [(t, n) for t, n in segs[0][2] if t < 0.5]
        for s in segs[1:]:
            s[2][:0] = [x for x in opening if x[0] < min(tt for tt, _ in s[2])]
    video(segs, lateral, window, rings=rings, after=after, enter=enter)
```

Second quarter, first-and-10. The running back takes the handoff, starts toward the right side of
the line, and is hit before he gets to it, by a defensive tackle who is already two yards into the
backfield. The replay shows the tackle lined up just outside the right guard and gone past him before
the guard has finished his first step. "He lives in the backfield," says the analyst. Two drives later,
the same offense runs right up the middle. This time the defender in the center of the line, the
biggest man on the field, doesn't go anywhere at all. The center hits him, a guard comes over to help,
and he simply stays where he is, two blockers leaning on him, until the running back arrives and he
throws one of them aside and makes the tackle. "He ate up two blockers," the analyst says. Two
defensive linemen, two opposite ways to be great: one wins by *going*, the other by *staying*. This
chapter is about why both exist, what each costs, and how to tell which one you are watching.

**You'll be able to:**

- Look at a defensive line before the snap and say what each player's alignment asks of him
  (nose, 3-technique, 4i, 4, 5-technique, 9, wide-9) and what kind of body the spot calls for.
- Tell one-gap from two-gap play by a lineman's first step, and say what each style buys the defense
  and what it gives up.
- Describe how a defensive lineman fights a down block, a reach block and a double team, and why each
  answer is what it is.
- Explain what it means to set the edge and to keep contain, and find the players doing it.
- Spot a slant or an angle at the snap, and say why the defense moved and where it is now vulnerable.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}

  D outward from the center), technique numbers (even numbers head-up on a blocker, odd numbers on his
  outside shoulder, an "i" on his inside shoulder: a **3-technique** is on a guard's outside shoulder, a
  **5** on a tackle's), *covered* and *uncovered* linemen, *play side* and *backside*, and the blocks this
  chapter's defenders have to beat: the down block, reach, cut-off, combo (double team), pull and kick-out.
- **[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)**: the
  **4-3** and **3-4** base defenses (four or three defensive linemen), the box, and edge rushers.

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and plays go up the
page. *Left* and *right* always mean the offense's left and right (page left and page right), in the
text as well as the pictures, even when we describe a defender's move. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five
offensive linemen (in the smallest diagrams just T, G and C), Y is a tight end, Q the quarterback and R
the running back. Defensive linemen are labelled with their **technique number** (a 3 is a
3-technique); M, W and S are the Mike, Will and Sam linebackers, and E is an *edge* player, an outside
linebacker standing up at the end of the line. Blue lines ending in a short bar are blocks; orange arrows
are where the defender goes; green letters are gaps, never players.

## The defensive lineman's three jobs

Watch a defensive lineman on a running play and it looks like a shoving match he either wins or
loses. It is more specific than that. On every snap he has three jobs, in order:

1. **Defeat the block.** A 300-pound man is coming at him, from the front, the side, or two at once.
   Before he can do anything else, he has to stop that man from moving him where the offense wants
   him to go.
2. **Control his gap.** Every defense gives each run defender a gap (or two) to be responsible for,
   so that wherever the ball carrier goes, someone is already there. A lineman who beats his blocker
   but ends up in the wrong place has won the fight and lost the play.
3. **Find the ball and get to it.** Only after the first two does he get to chase the ball carrier,
   and by then, on most runs, the ball carrier is already close.

The tension in defensive line play is between the first two jobs. A lineman who is *on* a blocker,
hands locked on him, can feel where the block is taking him and can hold his ground, but he is not
going anywhere fast. A lineman who is *in a gap*, shooting through the space beside the blocker,
can get into the backfield in a heartbeat, but if he guesses wrong about where the ball is going,
he has run himself out of the play. Every defense chooses, snap by snap and player by player,
which of those two to ask for. That choice has names, *one-gap* and *two-gap*, and they are the
spine of this chapter. First, though, look at *where* the linemen stand, because the alignment is
already half of the choice.

## The technique map, from the defense's side

In [The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) you learned the
technique numbers as a map the offensive line reads: which blocker has a man on him, which is free.
Now turn the map around. To a defensive coordinator, each number is a *job description*, and each job
wants a different kind of body.

``` {.python .cell-code}
from gridiron.data import nfl

ARCH = [  # (role, player, combine year, fallback height in inches, fallback weight)
    ("4i / 4 / 5", "J.J. Watt", 2011, 77, 290),
    ("Nose: 0 / 1", "Vince Wilfork", 2004, 73, 323),
    ("3-technique", "Aaron Donald", 2014, 73, 285),
    ("Edge: the 9", "T.J. Watt", 2017, 76, 252),
    ("Wide-9", "Jason Babin", 2004, 75, 260),
]
try:  # measurements from the nflverse combine file (cached in data/cache)
    comb = nfl().load_combine().to_pandas()
    def _inches(ht):
        f, i = str(ht).split("-")
        return int(f) * 12 + int(i)
    sizes = {}
    for role, name, yr, h, wt in ARCH:
        row = comb[(comb.player_name == name) & (comb.season == yr)].iloc[0]
        sizes[name] = (_inches(row.ht), float(row.wt))
except Exception:   # offline: the same numbers, typed in
    sizes = {name: (h, wt) for role, name, yr, h, wt in ARCH}


def silhouette(ax, x, y0, ht_in, wt, k=0.105, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, gain=2.4):
    """A standing figure: height to scale (k units per inch); width grows with pounds per inch of height,
    exaggerated by the power `gain` so a 70-pound difference is visible at print size."""
    H = ht_in * k
    f = ((wt / ht_in) / 3.9) ** gain
    head_r = 0.062 * H
    sh, hip = y0 + 0.80 * H, y0 + 0.47 * H
    tw_s, tw_h = 0.135 * H * f, 0.105 * H * f
    torso = Polygon([(x - tw_s, sh), (x + tw_s, sh), (x + tw_h, hip), (x - tw_h, hip)], closed=True)
    parts = [torso]
    lw_ = 0.07 * H * f
    for s in (-1, 1):   # legs
        parts.append(Polygon([(x + s * 0.012 * H, hip), (x + s * (0.012 * H + lw_ + 0.01 * H), hip),
                              (x + s * (0.012 * H + lw_ * 0.85), y0), (x + s * 0.02 * H, y0)], closed=True))
        aw = 0.045 * H * f   # arms
        parts.append(Polygon([(x + s * tw_s, sh), (x + s * (tw_s + aw), sh - 0.02 * H),
                              (x + s * (tw_h + aw * 1.3), y0 + 0.44 * H), (x + s * (tw_h + aw * 0.2), y0 + 0.45 * H)],

    return sh + 0.04 * H + 2 * head_r
```

### The nose: 0 and 1

The man over the center is the **nose**, the [nose tackle](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd)
of The Twenty-Two. He lines up in one of two ways. Head-up on the center he is a **0-technique**, and
nothing about his alignment tells the offense which side of the center he will play. On one of the
center's shoulders he is a **1-technique**, a *shade nose*, sitting in that side's A gap.

Either way, he is the player offenses most like to double-team. Look at where he stands: the center
in front of him and a guard on either side, all within a step. Two of those three can reach him
with no effort at all, and the combo block you met in
[03-01](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd), center and guard together, is aimed at men in
exactly his spot. So the nose's first quality is not speed but *mass and pad level*: getting lower than
the blocker, so that the blocker's push goes up into the nose's chest while the nose's push goes straight
through the blocker, and being heavy enough that two men leaning on him can't move him. That is why noses
are the heaviest players on the field. Vince Wilfork, the model for a generation of them, measured
6-foot-1 and 323 pounds at his Scouting Combine; modern noses such as the Eagles' Jordan Davis (341
pounds) and Dexter Lawrence (342), a Giant until an April 2026 trade sent him to Cincinnati, are just as
heavy and much taller.[^combine]

What does the defense get from a man who absorbs two blockers? Arithmetic. In
[hat math](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) the offense has a fixed number of blockers.
Every blocker spent on the nose is one who isn't climbing to a linebacker, and an unblocked
linebacker is a tackle waiting to happen. A great nose's best plays often show up in a linebacker's
tackle total, not his own.

### The 3-technique: the penetrator

You met the [**3-technique**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-technique) in
[03-01](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) as the alignment that became a position: a
defensive tackle on the guard's outside shoulder, in the B gap. What is new from the defense's side is
*why* the defense puts its best interior athlete there. The spot gives him the best odds of a single
blocker. The center is two men away and can't easily help. The tackle can, and against the run the
guard-tackle double team on a 3 is one of the most common blocks in football; but every snap the tackle
spends on him is a snap he isn't climbing to a linebacker or blocking the end, so the offense has to choose
which problem to leave alone. On passing downs the choice usually goes the 3's way: the center slides to
help the other guard, the tackle has the edge rusher, and the 3 gets the guard alone. So the defense puts
its quickest, most explosive interior player there, built to get off the ball and shoot the gap before the
guard can get his body in the way: Warren Sapp in the 1990s, Aaron Donald in the 2010s, both about
6-foot-1 or 6-foot-2 and listed at roughly 280 to 300 pounds, both much lighter than a nose and much
quicker.[^dtsize] Teams pay for that: in the contracts file in October 2026, the ten richest deals for
interior defensive linemen averaged about $31 million a year, more than any defensive position except
edge rushers.[^pay]

Which side does he line up on? That is the defense's choice, and it is usually made by a rule tied to the
offense's formation: many 4-3 teams put the 3-technique toward the tight end (the *Over* front), others
away from him (the *Under*), and some toward the wide side of the field or the running back. Spot the
rule and you can predict where the 3 will be before the offense breaks the huddle. The fronts and their
rules are in [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd).

The cost is the mirror image. A 3-technique who is moved off his spot by a double team, or who
shoots upfield and misses, leaves the B gap empty. That's the bargain one-gap football makes, and
we'll come back to it.

### The tackle's techniques: 4i, 4 and 5, the long men

Three alignments sit on the offensive tackle: the [**4i**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4i-technique)
on his inside shoulder, the 4 head-up on him, and the
[**5-technique**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-5-technique) on his outside shoulder. These are the
classic spots of the defensive ends in a three-man front, and the body they want is *long*: tall
players with long arms, around 290 to 310 pounds, who can lock out an offensive tackle at arm's length
and still see past him to the ball. J.J. Watt, 6-foot-5 and 290 at his combine, played the 5 for the
Houston Texans and turned it into a pass-rushing position: he led the league in sacks twice.[^jjwatt]

Each spot hints at a job, though the call has the final say. The **4**, head-up, is the classic
*two-gap* end of the old 3-4: he controls the tackle and owns the B and C gaps on either side of him. The
**5** usually owns the C gap he sits in. The **4i** usually owns the B gap he sits in, as a one-gapper,
but some defenses ask him to control the tackle and play the C gap too, so watch his first step.

Why the inside shoulder? 03-01 gave the offense's view: same gap as a 3, different blocker occupied. From
the defense's side the point is the blocking angles. On a zone run toward him, the guard has to reach a
man who is already outside *him*; on a run away, the tackle has to cut off a man who is already inside
*him*. And because the 4i can play off either blocker, he muddles which of them should take him and which
should climb. It is the end's favorite alignment in the *tite* fronts that NFL defenses use to stop
inside runs (five men on the line: three linemen in a 4i, a 0 and a 4i, plus two edge players standing
outside them), which you will meet in [Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd). The 5,
outside the tackle in the C gap, is the end's spot in four-man fronts as well, where, with no tight end on
his side, he is often the last man on the line and has the edge.

### The 9, the wide-9 and the edge

The 9 sits on the tight end's outside shoulder. Whoever lines up there is usually the defense's
[edge](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) on that side: in a 4-3 a defensive end, in a 3-4 an
outside linebacker standing up rather than in a three-point stance (T.J. Watt in Pittsburgh is the
type). He is lighter again, 250 to 270 pounds, because his two jobs both happen in space: rush the
passer around the tackle, and on runs, keep the ball from getting outside him. That second job is
called setting the edge, and it has its own section below.

Go wider still and you reach the most extreme alignment on the line, the
[**wide-9**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-9): a defensive end lined up well outside the tight
end, usually one to two or more yards beyond the tight end's outside shoulder (the exact width changes with
down and distance), or, with no tight end, just as far beyond where one would stand. He is usually in a
*sprinter's stance*: a three-point stance with his feet staggered and his weight well forward on his hand,
like a sprinter in the blocks, often tilted in toward the quarterback. The difference from a 9 is not a
new number but distance and posture: a 9 is close enough to touch the tight end and is ready to take him
on; a wide-9 is out of reach and ready only to run. The wide-9 exists for one reason: it gives a fast pass
rusher the best possible angle around the tackle. The tight end can't block him without help (he is too
far outside), and the tackle has to cover a lot of ground to meet him. The price is just as plain. With
the end that far out, the space between him and the next defender inside is enormous, and somebody,
usually a linebacker, has to fill it on runs.

The wide-9's modern history runs through one coach. Jim Washburn, the Tennessee Titans' defensive line
coach from 1999 to 2010 and the Philadelphia Eagles' in 2011 and 2012, built his lines around ends who
lined up wide and attacked upfield on every snap. He summed up his philosophy in a sentence: "I like fast
guys that play hard and attack." Gap assignments, he said, were not the point: the job was to "whip the
blocker and tackle the ballcarrier if he's in that gap or that gap. Just play football."[^washburn] Jim
Schwartz, the Titans' defensive coordinator for most of those years, carried the wide, attacking front to
Philadelphia and then Cleveland, where Myles Garrett set the single-season sack record of 23 in 2025,
though by then no defense lined up that way on every snap.[^schwartz] How the wide-9 fits into a whole
four-man front, and what it does to the linebackers behind it, is in [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd).

### The numbers this map leaves out

03-01's chart had a few more numbers. They exist, but you will see them less often, because each is a
compromise between two of the jobs above. The **2i** (the guard's inside shoulder) and the head-up **2**
put a man on a guard rather than the center: a 2i squeezes the A gap from outside, and some odd and
under fronts use one, but a lineman there is easy for the center and guard to double, without the 3's
one-on-one or the nose's mass to make it worth it. The **6** and **7** are head-up and on the inside
shoulder of a tight end: spots for a strong-side end whose first job is to stop the tight end from
blocking down on the linemen inside him. You will meet them in the front families of the next two chapters.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Every alignment is a trade between the run and the pass, and between size and speed.** Inside, where
blockers are close together and double teams are easy, the defense wants mass that can't be moved: the
nose. One step outside, where a defender can get a single blocker, it wants quickness: the 3-technique.
On the tackle, it wants length: the 4i, 4 and 5. On the edge, it wants speed, and the wider it aligns its
edge rusher the more pass rush it gets and the more run defense it gives up. When you read a front,
read it as a list of bets. Which spots did the defense fill with which kind of player, and what is it
hoping you'll do?
:::

## One-gap: attack a gap

Now the big choice. In a [**one-gap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-gap) defense, each
defensive lineman is responsible for exactly one gap. He lines up in it or shaded toward it (that is
what an odd number or an "i" usually signals), and at the snap he attacks it. His goal is
[**penetration**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-penetration): getting across the line of scrimmage
and into the offense's backfield before the play can develop, through his gap. If a blocker gets in
his way, he defeats the blocker *while staying in his gap*; he does not need to read where the ball is
going first, because the other gaps belong to somebody else.

How does he attack it? Watch three things, the same three a defensive line coach teaches first. His
*stance*: shaded toward his gap, with the hand and foot on the gap side slightly back, so his first step
goes straight into the gap instead of at the blocker. His *key*: he does not wait for the quarterback's
cadence (the defense never knows the snap count), so he watches the ball, or the blocker's hand beside it,
and moves the instant it moves. And his *hat and hands*: helmet into the gap he owns, hands on the
blocker's near shoulder or chest, pads lower than the blocker's, so that even if the blocker gets to him he
is driving through the gap rather than standing in front of the man.

That last point, staying in his gap, is what makes one-gap football work: **the gaps add up.** Seven gaps
across a line with one tight end, seven defenders in the box, one defender for each. The linemen take the
gaps they are aligned in; the linebackers behind them take the rest. Everybody has one job and can play it
fast. (Change the formation and the count changes with it: no tight end means six gaps, two tight ends
mean eight, and the defense adds or removes a box defender to keep one man per gap. The full accounting is
[Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).)

Here is a one-gap 3-technique doing his job. The offense runs outside zone to the right, the run from

before the reach can land. (If the guard does get there first, the 3 plays the reach the way every
defender does, the subject of *Fighting the blocks*, below.)

``` {.python .cell-code}
def one_gap_play():
    off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
                lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M")])
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    # the line steps right (outside zone): the guard steps sideways to reach the 3 and is late
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.6, 2.25), speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-1.3, 2.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (-0.1, 4.4), speed=3.4)              # uncovered: steps play side, then climbs
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.1, 3.9), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.0, 6.0), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, 6.6), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.5, 0.85), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "LG", (-0.4, -0.75), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.5, -2.35), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "L1", (0.95, 0.15), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "LE", (0.6, -3.2), "path", speed=1.2)
    # the 3-technique: get-off into the B gap, past the guard's hip, into the back's track
    go_to(p, "R3", (-0.45, 3.05), "path", speed=4.4, via=[(0.4, 2.85)])
    go_to(p, "R3", (-3.55, 3.45), "path", speed=4.8, via=[(-2.0, 3.4)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 3.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.2); go_to(p, "WILL", (3.6, 0.2), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.0, 0.7), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.15, 3.8), "run", speed=6.4, via=[(-6.6, 1.4)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.55)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.05, 3.85), "run", speed=0.8)
    return p


def mark_tfl(fld, play, t, i):
    if t >= 1.1:
        spot(fld, play, -4.3, 3.65, ms=9)


P_ONE = one_gap_play()
animation_or_strip([(P_ONE, 0.0, ""), (P_ONE, 0.2, ""), (P_ONE, 0.6, ""), (P_ONE, 1.15, "")],
                   notes=["the 3 on the RG's outside\nshoulder: he owns the B gap",
                          "get-off: first step into\nthe B gap, low",
                          "past the guard's hip before\nthe reach can land",
                          "in the back's path, 4 yards\ndeep: tackle for loss"],
                   rings=(("R3", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-5.4, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 6.2), after=mark_tfl,
                   width_in=5.2)
```

A one-gap 3-technique against outside zone to the right (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates; faint lines are each player's path so far). 1: the 3 (ringed) is on the right guard's outside shoulder; his gap is the B gap. 2: the [get-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-get-off), the defender's first-step explosion at the snap. The defense never knows the snap count, so he watches the ball and moves the instant it moves; his first step is already into the B gap while the guard is still stepping sideways to reach him and the tackle steps past him to climb to the Mike. 3: he is past the guard's hip before the guard can get his head across: penetration. 4: he meets the running back about four yards behind the line, in the back's path to the outside, before the back can turn upfield (X).
:::
:::


**Why it exists.** One-gap play turns the defense's linemen loose. A lineman who doesn't have to read
before he moves gets a half-step head start on every snap, and on the line half a step is everything:
the blocker who is reaching or pulling or setting for a pass is moving *sideways* or *backward* while
the defender is moving forward. The results are the plays fans remember, tackles for loss, sacks, a
running back hit as he takes the handoff, and they wreck an offense's plans in a way a two-yard gain
never does. One-gap play also fits the players the modern game produces. A lineman who wins by
quickness, the Donald type, is wasted standing still with his hands on a blocker; turn him loose in a
gap and he is the most disruptive player on the field.

**What it costs.** Three things.

- **A wrong guess is a big hole.** A one-gapper who penetrates *past* the play, or gets moved out of his
  gap by a double team, leaves his gap empty, and nobody else was assigned to it. A run that gets through
  a vacated gap is usually not a short gain, because the next defender is a linebacker who was busy with
  his own gap.
- **Offenses build plays to punish it.** An aggressive penetrator is exactly what the *trap* in
  [Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) is designed for: let him into the
  backfield unblocked, then hit him from the side with a pulling lineman, and run the ball through the
  space he left. Draws and screens work on the same idea: invite the rush, then go where it was.
- **It needs everyone else to be right.** One-gap defense is only as good as its accounting. If one
  linebacker fills the wrong gap, there are two defenders in one gap and none in another. That is why
  one-gap teams spend so much practice time on *run fits*, the subject of
  [Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

**Where it came from.** For much of football's history, defensive linemen were taught to read and
react. The great attacking interior linemen changed that by being too quick to keep at home. The best
known story is Pittsburgh's in 1974: late that season the Steelers began lining Joe Greene up at the
center, his stance tilted at about 45 degrees toward the A gap, so he could knife through before anyone
could block him. Accounts differ on whose idea it was: the Hall of Fame credits Greene, other histories
credit his line coach, George Perles. The Steelers called it the *stunt 4-3* (a period name: today
"stunt" usually means the looping pass-rush games of [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd),
which this was not). It began as a practice-field experiment, got its
first heavy use late that regular season, and carried the Steelers through the 1974 playoffs to their
first Super Bowl win.[^greene] Two decades later the Tampa Bay
Buccaneers of Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin built a whole defense around a one-gap 3-technique, Warren
Sapp, who was the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year in 1999.[^sapp]

## Two-gap: control the man, then pick a side

The other answer is older, heavier and quieter. In a [**two-gap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-gap)
defense, a lineman lines up [head-up](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-head-up) on a blocker (a 0, a 2,
a 4: the even numbers) and is responsible for the gaps on *both* sides of him. At the snap he does not
attack a gap. He attacks the *man*: strikes him with both hands inside the blocker's chest, straightens
his arms to keep the blocker off his body (coaches call it *locking out*), and stands him up at the line
of scrimmage. Then, with the blocker held at arm's length, he looks into the backfield, sees which side
the ball is going, and throws the blocker the other way to make the tackle.

Coaches have a rule for how a two-gapper knows which way to go: **read the blocker's head.** A blocker
who wants to wall a defender off from one side has to get his helmet to that side of him. Say the center's
helmet slides to the right of the nose (the offense's right, as always in this book): the center is trying
to keep him from going right, which means the ball is going right. So the two-gapper "plays across the
face": he keeps his arms locked, works to the side the blocker's head went (right), throws the blocker the
other way (left), and is standing in the right A gap when the ball arrives. The block tells him where the
ball is going before he ever sees the ball.

Head-up is the natural spot for this, because the defender starts with a gap on each side and the blocker
in the middle. A *shaded* player can be asked to two-gap too, and some 4-3 teams ask exactly that of a 1 or
a 4i. He plays it the same way, by striking and controlling the man he is shaded on, but his near gap is
already his and his far gap is the hard one: to reach it he has to work back across the blocker's face, so
his alignment is a lean, not a commitment. That is why "odd number or an i" is only a hint about the job.

::: {#cell-fig-two-gap-nose .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def two_gap_play(side=+1):
    """3-4 with a 0 nose and 4-technique ends against inside zone right. The center and right guard
    double the nose and the left guard climbs; the back hits the right A (side=+1) or cuts back to
    the left A (side=-1)."""
    off = line("full") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
    dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
                lbs=[("MIKE", 4.6, -2.2, "M"), ("WILL", 4.6, 2.2, "W")])
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    # the strike: nose and center meet, the nose locks out and drives him back a step
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.3, 0.0), speed=1.2, via=[(-0.6, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.75, 0.0), "path", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.6, 0.05), "path", speed=0.6)
    # the right guard doubles the nose (the drive man, from the side); the left guard climbs to the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.35, 1.0), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.55, 1.4)])
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.75, -2.6), speed=3.6, via=[(0.5, -1.6)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.85, -1.75), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.2)
    # the ends hold up the tackles
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.2, -3.2), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "LE", (1.0, -3.2), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.4), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, 3.4), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 0.4), "path", speed=3.6)          # opens to the play side for the handoff
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.7, -1.9), "path", speed=2.4)         # then carries out his fake
    if side > 0:   # the hole never opens; the free Will fills it
        go_to(p, "NT", (0.55, 0.3), "path", speed=0.5, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (-0.75, 2.45), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.15)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.55, 1.9), "run", speed=5.6, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-3.2, 1.2)])
    else:          # cutback: the nose throws the center right and takes the left A
        go_to(p, "NT", (-0.25, -1.05), "path", speed=3.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "C", (-1.45, 0.45), speed=1.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (2.6, 0.8), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.4)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.25, -1.3), "run", speed=5.6, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-3.2, 0.1)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.45)
    return p


def two_gap_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    """Both A gaps marked while the nose still owns them; the locked-out arms; an X at the tackle."""
    if t < 0.2:
        for w in (-0.8, 0.8):
            gap_tag(fld, play, -3.2, w, "A", fontsize=7)
    (nd, nw), (cd, cw) = play.position("NT", t), play.position("C", t)
    if 0.3 <= t and abs(nw - cw) < 0.5 and nd - cd > 1.2:      # arms locked out on the center
        for off in (-0.38, 0.38):
            xs, ys = _P(fld, play, np.array([nd - 0.7, cd + 0.5]), np.array([nw + off, cw + off]))
            fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=11)
    if t >= 1.1:
        if play.position("RB", 2.0)[1] > 0:
            spot(fld, play, -1.65, 2.2, ms=9)
        else:
            spot(fld, play, -1.25, -1.2, ms=9)


P_TWO_R, P_TWO_L = two_gap_play(+1), two_gap_play(-1)
animation_or_strip([(P_TWO_R, 0.0, ""), (P_TWO_R, 0.45, ""), (P_TWO_R, 1.25, "ball right"),
                    (P_TWO_L, 1.25, "ball left")],
                   notes=["0-technique on the C:\nboth A gaps are his",
                          "strike and lock out; the RG\ncomes over to double him",
                          "he gives no ground: the RG is\nstuck, the W is free to tackle",
                          "same start, back cuts left:\nhe sheds the C and tackles"],
                   rings=(("NT", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-5.8, 5.8), window=(-7.8, 6.4), after=two_gap_marks,
                   width_in=5.0)
```

A two-gap nose tackle in a 3-4 against an inside zone run, the same start with two endings (simulated, Big Data Bowl coordinates). 1: the nose (ringed) is a 0-technique, head-up on the center, responsible for both A gaps (green). Nobody covers the guards. 2: the strike. Both hands inside the center's chest, arms locked out (the two short bars), the center held a yard off his body and pushed back a step. The right guard comes over to double-team him, as the zone rules tell him to, while the left guard climbs to the Mike. 3: the back aims at the right A gap. The nose gives no ground, so the hole never opens, and the right guard can't leave the double team to block the Will: the Will, unblocked, fills and makes the tackle (X). 4: the same play, but the back cuts back to the left A gap, so the nose throws the center off to the right and makes the tackle in the left A himself. Either way the offense spent two blockers on one man and the run went nowhere.
:::
:::


**Why it exists.** Look back at the right half of @fig-gap-accounting. If one lineman can be responsible
for two gaps, three linemen can hold six of them, and the defense has players left over. In the classic
two-gap 3-4, the two inside linebackers have no gap of their own to *rush to* at the snap. They read the
play and fill wherever the ball goes, and the two-gappers' job is to make that possible. Three linemen
can't occupy five blockers just by standing there: the guards are uncovered, and if nothing stops them
they climb straight to the linebackers. What stops them is the nose. A nose who can't be moved by the
center alone forces a guard to stay and help him, as in @fig-two-gap-nose, so at most one blocker gets up
to the linebackers, and the 4s keep the tackles from climbing at all. That is the two-gapper's real
product: not tackles, but *clean linebackers*. And because he doesn't commit before the snap, the offense
can't build its blocking around where he will go.

Two-gapping matters even more in the modern NFL than its reputation suggests. Defenses now keep two deep
safeties on many snaps to stop the pass, which leaves only six men in the box against an offense that may
have six or seven blockers ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
has the numbers). With six defenders and seven gaps, the accounting of one-gap football does not add up.
The usual fix is to ask a big nose to play both A gaps, so six men can cover seven gaps. That is one of
the ideas behind the light-box fronts of Vic Fangio and his followers, taken up in
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) and the case study
[Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).

**What it costs.**

- **Rare bodies.** Holding a 310-pound center at arm's length while a guard hits you from the side takes
  size and strength that very few people have: two-gap noses are typically well over 320 pounds, and the pool
  of such players who can also move is small.[^pffnose]
- **No head start.** Reading before moving means the two-gapper is always reacting. He rarely makes a
  tackle behind the line and rarely gets a sack. On a pass his job is mostly to push the center straight
  back into the quarterback's lap, collapsing the middle of the pocket so the quarterback can't step up,
  which matters but doesn't show up as a sack. That is why classic two-gap noses often leave the field on
  third down for a lighter, quicker pass-rush package.
- **His value hides.** The stat sheet credits the man who makes the tackle, not the man who made the tackle
  possible. A great two-gapper can have a quiet box score in a game he dominated.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A 3-4 means two-gap, and a 4-3 means one-gap." It is a decent first guess, nothing more. The classic
3-4s of the 1970s through the 2000s, Bill Parcells's and Bill Belichick's among them, did two-gap with
big ends and a big nose. But Wade Phillips, son of the Bum Phillips who devised the technique numbers,
spent decades running an *attacking*, one-gap 3-4: when he took over the Houston Texans' defense in 2011,
the team's own preview called it "his one-gap scheme," and the line coach explained that it was "not like a
two-gap type defense where you need that 350-pound nose man to be able to just clog up and take on two
blocks."[^phillips34] And plenty of 4-3 teams ask a nose to two-gap. The number
of linemen tells you how many there are; their first step tells you how they play.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, a defensive lineman is mostly someone you steer at the quarterback, and the run defense takes
care of itself. On a real early down, a lineman's job is mostly the gap: hold it, or attack it, exactly as
the call says. A nose tackle who abandons both A gaps to chase a sack can give up a 20-yard run even if he
beats his man, which is why defensive line coaches grade every snap on assignment before they grade it on
result.
:::

## Fighting the blocks

Whichever style he plays, a defensive lineman has to beat whatever block the offense throws at him, and
the offense has a whole vocabulary of them. You learned them from the blocker's side in
[03-01](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd). Here are the defender's answers to the three
that matter most, the down block, the reach and the double team, and the one principle underneath all of
them: **fight pressure with pressure.** Whatever direction a block is pushing you, push back into it. A
blocker pushes you *where the offense wants you*, toward the hole's edge or out of your gap, so leaning
into the pressure is how you stay where the defense wants you.

### Against a down block

A [down block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-block) hits a defender from the side: the blocker
outside him comes inside, at an angle, to drive him toward the center and seal the inside of the hole.
Two defenders are involved, and they have opposite jobs.

- **The man being down-blocked** (the 3-technique in panel 1) feels pressure from his outside. If he
  gives way, he is washed down the line and the hole doubles in size. So he fights pressure: drops his
  outside shoulder into the blocker and pushes back outward, holding his gap and never slipping behind
  the block. A few defenses let a dominant player fight *across* the blocker's face and into the hole
  himself; if he doesn't win that fight, he has given up the inside.
- **The man left alone** (the 5 in panel 1) has just seen the tackle in front of him leave. A blocker who
  vanishes is a warning, not a gift. On a gap-scheme run like power, the tackle blocks down *because*
  someone else is coming for the end: a pulling guard or a fullback, to kick him out. So he **squeezes**:
  steps down the line, hip to hip with the down-blocker, shrinking the hole, with his eyes inside for
  the puller. When the puller arrives, the defense's call decides what he does next. He can keep his
  outside arm free and force the ball back inside (*box* or *squeeze*), or attack the puller's inside
  shoulder and pile up the hole, pushing the ball outside to a teammate waiting there (*spill*, the
  "wrong-arm" you met in [03-03](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)). Which one, and who
  is waiting, is the heart of [Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

There is a cousin of this rule that every defensive line coach teaches: **if nobody blocks you, something
is coming.** A lineman who is let through untouched should close inside at once and *get small*: turn his
shoulders and drop his pads, so a blocker coming from the side has only a narrow shoulder to hit and can't
knock him out of the gap. The likeliest explanation is a trap block from the side, the gap play built to
catch penetrators. But coaches say "trap *or read*," because there is a second explanation. On an option
play the offense leaves an end unblocked on purpose and lets the quarterback read him
([Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd)): if the end closes inside, the
quarterback keeps the ball and runs where he was. How does a lineman know which it is? Partly from what he
sees (a quarterback holding the ball in the back's belly with his eyes on him is reading him; a guard
pulling toward him is trapping him), and mostly from the call. The call tells him in advance whether he
takes the back or the quarterback, and against option teams defenses often swap those jobs between the
end and a linebacker, the [scrape exchange](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scrape-exchange) of 03-04,
precisely so the read is wrong.

### Against a reach

A [reach block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reach-block) is the blocker trying to get his head
and body *outside* a defender who is already a step to the play side of him, and seal him inside. The
defender's whole job is not to let that happen, and he has the head start. A one-gapper fast enough to be
through his gap before the blocker arrives beats the reach before it starts, as in
@fig-one-gap-penetration. Once the blocker *has* got to him, every defender, one-gap or two-gap, does the
same thing: he steps with the blocker, keeps his *outside* arm free (so there is always an arm between the
blocker and the sideline), and presses the blocker back into the backfield. Panel 2 shows the effect: the
runner, who wanted to turn upfield just outside the guard, has to keep running sideways. Every yard he goes
sideways is a yard of pursuit for the rest of the defense.

The mistake to avoid is the one that looks most athletic: running *around* the block. A defender who
loops around the blocker's back to get outside him has left his gap. On outside zone, that is exactly
the hole the runner is looking for when he cuts back. The rule coaches use is to beat the block
*through* the blocker, not around him.

### Against a double team

The [double team](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-team), or combo block, is the hardest thing a
defensive lineman faces and the most important to survive. Two blockers want two things from him: to
move him off the ball, and then, once the linebacker behind him commits, for one of them to come off
and block that linebacker. The defender's goal is to deny both.

- **Don't get moved.** He widens his base, sinks his hips, and fights the pressure of the blocker coming
  from the side. Coaches call that blocker the *drive* man (he does the moving) and the one in front of the
  defender the *post* man (he stops him from going forward). The defender drops the hip nearest the drive
  man and leans into him, so the pair can't turn his shoulders and walk him out of his gap. Giving up a
  yard backward is how a double team creates the hole.
- **Keep both blockers.** The longer he keeps both men busy, the longer the linebacker behind him goes
  unblocked. The double team's second blocker is supposed to climb to the second level; a defender who
  stays heavy on him keeps him from leaving.
- **If he is losing, make a pile.** A lineman being driven back is taught to drop his hips, even to go to
  a knee in the gap, so that the bodies pile up where the hole was supposed to be. It looks like losing.
  It is a win if the running back has nowhere to go.

A few great linemen *split* double teams, slipping between the two blockers into the backfield, and it
is a spectacular play when it works. It is also a gamble. If he doesn't get through, he has turned his
shoulders and left his gap, and the double team walks him out of it.

### Against blocks going away

When the play goes away from a defender, his blocker uses a [cut-off block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cut-off-block)
(or the whole backside line *scoops*), stepping toward the play to get between him and the ball. Here he
does chase. He flattens down the line, staying at about the depth of the ball, so that if the runner cuts
back he is waiting. Backside blockers on zone runs often [cut](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cut-block)
him instead, diving at his thighs to put him on the ground; he plays the cut with his hands, pushing the
blocker's shoulders down and away, and keeps his feet free. But the defender farthest from the play has a
different rule, and it comes next.

## Setting the edge and keeping contain

The last man on the line on each side has a special job. Inside him, his teammates can count on someone
being in the gap next to them. Outside him there is nobody, just the sideline. If a run gets outside him,
it gets outside everybody.

To [**set the edge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-set-the-edge) is to be that last man and win: take
on the blocker coming at you (a tight end, a tackle, a pulling guard, a fullback) at or near the line of
scrimmage, with your outside arm free, and don't let him push you back or get his head outside you.
Then the run has only one place to go, back inside, toward the linebackers and safeties chasing it. A
defense talks about a *hard* edge (the defender holds his ground at the line and turns the ball in quickly)
and a *soft* edge (he gets pushed back or upfield, and the runner gets around him). Setting a hard edge is
one of the least glamorous and most valued skills an edge player has, and it is a big part of why teams
still want 270-pound defensive ends when a 245-pound linebacker might rush the passer just as well.
On a given play, the player who turns the ball back inside is also called the *force* defender; who that
is, and how it changes with the coverage, is in [Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

The end who did both jobs as well as anyone was **Reggie White**, the "Minister of Defense," who played for
the Eagles and the Packers and retired with 198 sacks, then the NFL record (Bruce Smith later passed him).
In Super Bowl XXXI, after the 1996 season, he sacked Drew Bledsoe three times, a Super Bowl record that has
since been tied but never broken, as Green Bay beat New England 35–21.[^white] If you find his games, watch
the runs at him rather than the sacks: the blocker in front of him going backward, White's outside arm
free, and the ball carrier turning back inside. That is a hard edge, from a man who was also one of the
great pass rushers of his era: proof that an edge player doesn't always have to choose between the two jobs.

[**Contain**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain) is the edge player's other rule, and its spirit is
the same: *nothing gets outside me*, but with an emphasis on patience. On the backside of a run, the end
who has contain does not chase the play flat down the line. He trails it at about the depth of the ball,
because the plays most likely to come back his way are the ones designed to punish a chasing end: the
bootleg, the reverse, the quarterback keeping the ball on a read
([Perimeter and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) has those plays
from the offense's side). Not every call keeps the end outside, though: against teams that run the read
option, the end is often told to crash on the running back while a linebacker loops outside him to take the
quarterback, the scrape exchange from the trap-or-read discussion above, a swap built to confuse the read.
Contain still belongs to *somebody*; the call says who. On a pass rush, contain means the ends rush outside
the tackles but not past the quarterback's depth. An end who loops too far upfield opens a lane between
himself and the quarterback, and a mobile quarterback steps up and runs through it. You will hear analysts
call this *rush-lane discipline*; how pass rushers balance it against getting home is in
[The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd).

Both jobs ask a fast, aggressive player to be patient on a down when patience isn't rewarded with a
statistic. That is exactly why offenses attack them. A defensive end who gets a little too eager for the
sack or the tackle for loss is the end the bootleg is built for.

## Line movement: slants and angles

So far the linemen have played from where they lined up. But the alignment the offense sees before the
snap doesn't have to be the one it blocks after the snap. Defenses can *move* their linemen at the snap,
and the two basic movements are the slant and the angle.

A [**slant**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant-line-movement) is a called movement in which the
linemen step hard across the face of the blocker in front of them at the snap, into the next gap over,
usually all in the same direction, gaining only a little ground: the slanter's job is to *arrive in the
next gap*, not to go deep. The linebackers move the opposite way to fill the gaps the line just left, so
the whole front's gap assignments shift by one. An
[**angle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-angle-line-movement) is a shorter movement, typically by one
or two linemen: a step at about 45 degrees into the adjacent gap that moves the defender over while he
keeps going *upfield*. Think of the slant as relocating the line, and the angle as a penetrator changing
lanes. (The words are not standardized. Some staffs call every movement a slant, some have names for a
slant toward the tight end and a slant away from him, and inward and outward moves by pairs of linemen
are often called a *pinch* and an *open*. The footwork varies by staff too: the clinic source cited here
starts the slant with a roughly 45-degree step that gains a little ground, and nearly every coach warns
that a lineman who moves purely sideways can be caught by the blocker and pushed along the line. What
separates the two movements is where the lineman is headed, across the line or through it.)[^movement]

**Why move?** Because the offense's blocking is decided before the snap. Every offensive lineman has
looked at the front and decided whether he is covered or uncovered, who doubles whom and who climbs to
which linebacker. Movement changes the answers after it is too late to change the call. A slant can turn
a covered lineman uncovered and an uncovered one covered in a single step. A double team aimed at a 3-technique
hits air when the 3 angles into the A gap. A pulling guard runs into a defender who wasn't in his path a
moment ago. Movement is also how a defense of quick, lighter linemen deals with bigger blockers: they
can't win a head-on shove, so they don't take one. As one college staff put it in a coaching clinic,
"we use a lot of slants up front (gap control) to try and keep the offensive linemen occupied, which then
will allow our linebackers the freedom to roam and get to the ball."[^movementwhy]

**What it costs.** Movement is a bet on where the play is going, and whether the bet pays depends on the
blocking scheme as much as the direction.

- **Against gap schemes**, slanting toward the run is the jackpot. Power and counter are built on pre-snap
  assignments and pullers aimed at where the defenders *were*; a front that slants into the play's path
  arrives at the hole before the blockers do, and the puller finds a defender where his gap was supposed to
  be. Slant *away* from a gap play and every defender has stepped out of the gap the ball is coming through,
  with the replacing linebackers a step farther from it.
- **Against zone**, slanting toward the run gains less than it looks. Zone linemen block whoever arrives in
  their area, so a slanting defender just runs into the next blocker's arms
  ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) explains why), and the play side gets crowded
  without getting stopped. The real danger is *behind* the slant: every lineman has left a gap, and the
  zone back's cutback is aimed at exactly those gaps. Against zone, a slant lives or dies on the linebackers
  replacing the gaps the line left.
- **Either way, the linebackers have to move with the line every time.** If one of them forgets the slant was
  called, two players fill one gap and the other is empty.

When two linemen go further and *loop* around each other on a pass rush, the movement becomes a stunt,
which belongs to [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd).

**How do the linemen know, and can you see it coming?** The call comes from the sideline to the defense's
[green-dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) player, usually a linebacker, who relays it in the
huddle or, against a fast offense, with a word or a hand signal at the line. It includes the front (where
each lineman lines up), whether each plays one gap or two, and any movement, and it can be changed at the
line when the offense shifts. From the stands or the couch you can sometimes see it leak. Look for the
[tells](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tell) you learned for offensive linemen in
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), applied to the other side
of the ball: a lineman whose stance is cheated (weight leaning, back foot staggered toward the gap he is
about to take, his body tilted the way Joe Greene's was), a lineman who widens or tightens his alignment
just before the snap, or a linebacker creeping toward the gap he will have to replace. Good defenses know
this and try to give the same look on every snap, so treat any tell as odds, not a promise.

## Putting a front together

Step back and the parts fit together. A defensive coordinator calling a front is choosing, for each
lineman, three things you can now name:

1. **Where he lines up** (his technique), which tells the offense who is covered and shapes its blocking.
2. **How he plays it**: one-gap (attack the gap he is in) or two-gap (control the man and read).
3. **Whether he moves**: straight ahead, or a slant or an angle into another gap at the snap.

Different answers to those questions are what separate the fronts in the rest of this part: the even
fronts with their 3-techniques and wide ends ([Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd)), the odd and tite
fronts with their 0s and 4is ([Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)), and the
linebackers whose jobs change with every one of these choices
([Linebackers and the Second Level](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)). A defense can also mix them:
two-gap the nose, one-gap the 3-technique, angle the end. The modern NFL front is less a system than a
menu.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Super Bowl XXXVII (2002 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl XXXVII, January 26, 2003: Tampa Bay 48, Oakland 21. The Buccaneers' defense,
built by Tony Dungy and coordinator Monte Kiffin around a one-gap four-man line and still run by Kiffin
in Jon Gruden's first season, intercepted the league MVP, Rich Gannon, a Super Bowl-record five times and
returned three of them for touchdowns.[^sb37] Warren Sapp played the 3-technique, and the design of that whole
defense, a fast, light front backed by linebackers who ran to the ball, starts with him.

**What to notice:**

- Find Sapp before each snap. He moves to whichever side the front's rule puts the 3-technique; note
  where the tight end is, see whether you can work out the rule, and notice which guard has a one-on-one
  problem.
- His first step. Count how often he is across the line of scrimmage before the guard in front of him
  has finished his first step. That is one-gap penetration at its purest.
- What happens behind him. When an offense spends a second blocker on him, look for the linebacker that
  blocker would have taken, and watch him run free.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England Patriots, 2004–2010 seasons"}
**The player:** Vince Wilfork, a first-round pick in 2004 who played nose tackle in Bill Belichick's
two-gap 3-4 for his first seven seasons: as a rookie he shared the job with the veteran Keith Traylor,
and from 2005 it was his alone. (In 2010 he spent some weeks at end, and in 2011 the Patriots went to a
four-man front.)[^wilfork] He was a Pro Bowler five times and won two Super
Bowls, XXXIX and XLIX.

**What to do:** pick any Patriots early-down base snap from those seasons in which Wilfork lines up over
the center. Ignore the ball and watch only him and the center.

- The strike: both hands inside, arms locked, the center held off his body.
- The double team: when a guard comes over, does Wilfork give ground? Usually he doesn't, and the
  linebacker behind him is unblocked.
- The shed: watch him throw the blocker to the side the ball isn't going. Then check the box score; his
  name often isn't in it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams, Super Bowl LVI (2021 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl LVI, February 13, 2022, at SoFi Stadium: Rams 23, Bengals 20. Cincinnati got the
ball back with 1:25 left needing a field goal to tie. Facing third-and-1 near midfield, the Bengals ran
Samaje Perine, and Aaron Donald and nose tackle Greg Gaines tackled him for no gain. On fourth-and-1,
Donald got to Joe Burrow and wrapped him up as he threw; the pass fell incomplete, and the Rams won.[^sb56]

**What to notice:** two snaps, one player, both phases of the game. On third down, a run: watch Donald's
[get-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-get-off), his first step at the instant the ball moves, and where he
is relative to the line when the back arrives. On fourth down, a pass: the same
first step, and the same result, a quarterback with no time. It is the best two-play summary of why
teams pay a one-gap 3-technique more than almost anyone else on the defense.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2011"}
**The season:** Jim Washburn's first year coaching the Eagles' defensive line, and the clearest look at a
full-time wide-9 front. The Eagles tied for the league lead with 50 sacks, and Jason Babin, whom Washburn had
also coached in Tennessee, had 18 of them.[^eagles2011]

**What to notice:** the ends' alignment, well outside the tight end on that side (or where one would be),
in sprinter's stances; how quickly they are upfield; and then, on running plays, the space inside them.
Watch which linebacker has to fill the lane between the end and the 3-technique, and how often he gets
there in time. The pass rush and the run lanes come from the same alignment: that is the trade this
chapter has been describing, on the field for a whole season.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap: find the 3-technique.**

- Look at the guards. Is there a defensive tackle on a guard's *outside* shoulder? That is the
  3-technique, and his side of the line is where the defense has put its quickness. Is he toward the tight
  end or away from him? That is the front's rule, and it will usually hold all game. Is there one big man
  right over the center? That is a 0 nose, likely playing both A gaps.
- Look at the ends. On the tackle (a 4i, 4 or 5)? Standing up just outside the tight end (a 9)? Way out
  wide, a couple of yards past the tight end or where one would be, in a sprinter's stance (a wide-9)? Wider
  ends mean more pass rush and bigger run lanes inside them.
- Don't try to measure a yard on the live shot. As in 03-01, ask *whose shoulder* the defender is on: the
  guard's outside shoulder is a 3, the tackle's inside shoulder a 4i, his outside shoulder a 5. The
  end-zone replay, shot straight down the line, shows it best.

**At the snap: the first step.**

- Does the lineman's first step go *into a gap*, upfield (one-gap), or *into the blocker*, with his hands,
  standing him up (two-gap)?
- Does the whole line step sideways together at the snap? That is a slant; look for the linebackers to shift
  the other way. One man darting into the next gap and on upfield while the rest go straight is an angle.

**After the play: where did the run go?**

- Which way did the run go relative to the 3-technique: at him, or away? Did he get into the backfield, get
  double-teamed, or get trapped?
- Did the run get outside the edge? If it did, ask who had the edge on that side and whether he got hooked.
  On a bootleg or scramble, ask who had contain.

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
before each early-down snap, note which side the 3-technique is on. After the play, note whether the run went
toward him or away from him. A few quarters of that will tell you something about both coordinators.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Read the bodies, not just the numbers.** Two fronts against the same one-tight-end offense, before
the snap, with the weights of the interior linemen shown. Neither is the one-gap or two-gap front from
@fig-gap-accounting. For each, say which linemen you expect to attack a gap and which to control a blocker and

``` {.python .cell-code}
fronts = [("Front A", front([("L4", "4i", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("R4", "4i", 1)],

                             others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.6, "E")]),
           [("NT", "330 lb"), ("L4", "300 lb"), ("R4", "300 lb")]),
          ("Front B", front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
                             lbs=[("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.0, "M"), ("SAM", 4.3, 4.4, "S")]),
           [("L1", "340 lb"), ("R3", "285 lb")])]
for ax, (ttl, dfn, wts) in zip(axes, fronts):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0, "R")], dfn, los=40,
             to_go=10)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.8), window=(-7.6, 6.8), title=False)
    for key, txt in wts:
        q = p.players[key]
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Front A is a mix: the nose two-gaps, the 4is most likely one-gap.** The 0 is head-up on the center with
no gap of his own, and he is 330 pounds: everything about him says *control the center and play both A
gaps*. The 4is are shaded into the B gaps, so the likeliest job is to own those (some defenses ask them to
play the C gap as well; their first step will tell you). Add it up: the nose holds two gaps, the 4is one each,
the edge players the outside gaps, and one inside linebacker fills the gap left over inside the tight end. The
other linebacker is the free one. That is the point of this front, which you will meet as the *tite* front in
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd): one big two-gapper lets six men cover
seven gaps against the run, so the defense can keep two safeties deep.

**Front B is shaded like a one-gap front, but look at the nose.** The 3-technique is a classic penetrator (285
pounds, in the B gap): expect him to attack. The 1-technique is shaded too, but 340 pounds is an anchor's body,
not a penetrator's. Whatever the call says about his gaps, his job is to take on the center and the guard and
not move, which keeps a blocker off the Mike. So: the 3 and the ends attack their gaps, the nose holds his
ground, and if the nose eats a double team, the Mike is the man who runs free.

**The lesson:** alignment is a strong hint and body type is another. Wade Phillips ran a one-gap defense out of
3-4 looks for decades, and many 4-3 teams ask a big shaded nose to anchor or play both A gaps. Confirm it with the
first step after the snap: into the gap, or into the man.
:::
:::
