::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely back to the left, on the cutback, and the linebackers decide it.** The slant ran the same way as
the play. Inside zone's blockers are happy about that at first: each one simply rides the man who slanted into
his area (the right guard takes the 1 who came into the right A gap, the right tackle the 3 who went to the
right C). But look at what moved. The 3 left the right B gap, which is exactly the gap the back is aiming at,
and the 1 left the left A gap. The 5 left the left C gap for the left B.

Replacing those gaps is the linebackers' job, and they have to move the opposite way from the line. **The Sam
has to get into the right B gap the 3 vacated.** If he doesn't, the back runs through it untouched. If he does,
the back does what inside zone teaches him: he *bends* the run back toward the gaps the slant emptied. **The Mike
has the left A** and **the Will the left C** the 5 left. If either flows right with the line instead of filling
behind it, the cutback lane is empty and the next defender is a safety. That is the bet every slant makes against
zone: the line wins the first half-second, and the linebackers have to win the rest.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The two ends have contain: the 5 on the left and the wide-9 on the right.** Their rule is to rush *outside* the
tackles but not *past* the quarterback's depth. If either one runs a wide arc around the tackle and keeps going,
he ends up behind the quarterback, and the space between him and the defensive tackle next to him becomes a
running lane. A mobile quarterback steps up into the pocket and out through that lane, usually for a first down
on third-and-7.

**The wide-9 is the likeliest to get it wrong**, because his whole alignment is built for a long, fast arc to the
quarterback. Against a runner he has to flatten his rush earlier and stay level with the quarterback. The two
inside rushers have the opposite job: push the middle of the pocket back into the quarterback so he can't step up.
A four-man rush against a mobile quarterback is a box: two sides that must hold, and a front that must squeeze.
When one side bursts, look for the quarterback there. Defenses facing a real runner often go further: all four
rushers stay level with the quarterback and squeeze him instead of racing to him (a
[mush rush](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mush-rush)), or one defender is held back to shadow him (a
[spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy)). [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) has the
rest of this, including the stunts that trade one rusher's lane for another's.
:::
:::

## Back to the replay

The chapter opened with two great defensive linemen on the same afternoon. Now you can name them.

- *Lined up just outside the right guard and gone past him before the guard finished his first step*: a
  one-gap **3-technique**. His alignment gave him a single blocker and the B gap; his get-off beat the reach
  before it landed; he was through the gap and in the back's path before the play could develop. That is
  penetration, and the analyst's "he lives in the backfield" is its signature.
- *The biggest man on the field, over the center, a guard comes over to help, and he stays where he is*: a
  two-gap **nose**. The center and guard double-teamed him, he gave no ground, and when the back arrived he
  shed one blocker to the side the ball went and made the tackle. "He ate up two blockers" is the other half of
  the story: on a play he doesn't finish himself, that guard never reaches the linebacker, who does.

One wins by going and one by staying, and both are doing the same arithmetic: making the offense's blockers
add up to less than the defense's gaps.

## Takeaways

- **Alignment is a job description.** The nose (0 or 1) anchors against double teams and wants mass; the
  3-technique is the likeliest to get a guard one-on-one and wants quickness; the 4i, 4 and 5 want length to control a tackle; the
  9 and the wide-9 want speed, and the wider the end, the more pass rush and the bigger the run lane inside him.
- **One-gap attacks.** Each lineman owns one gap and attacks it, aiming for penetration. It wins with quickness,
  creates sacks and tackles for loss, and turns the linemen loose, but a wrong guess leaves an empty gap, and traps,
  draws and screens are built to punish it.
- **Two-gap controls.** A head-up lineman strikes the blocker, locks out, reads (the blocker's head tells him where
  the ball is going) and sheds to the ball's side. One man covering two gaps, and forcing a second blocker to stay
  on him, keeps the linebackers clean, at the cost of rare bodies, little pass rush, and a stat sheet that hides
  his value.
- **Fight pressure with pressure.** Against a down block, the man blocked fights back outward and the man left alone
  squeezes and looks for the puller (or, if nobody blocks him at all, asks "trap or read?"); against a reach, step
  with the blocker and keep the outside arm free; against a double team, lean into the drive man, give no ground and
  keep both blockers.
- **The edge is everybody's boundary.** Setting the edge turns runs back inside; contain keeps the quarterback and
  the misdirection plays from getting outside. Both ask an aggressive player for patience.
- **Movement changes the picture after the snap.** Slants shift the whole line a gap; angles move one man while he
  keeps attacking. Both beat pre-snap blocking assignments, especially gap schemes, and both are bets on direction
  that the linebackers have to back up, above all against zone's cutback.

**Penetration, measured.** Tracking data turns this chapter's distinction into a number. A one-gap penetrator is
*behind* the line of scrimmage a second after the snap; a two-gapper is *at* it. In the two simulated plays above,
here is how far each ringed defender is past the line (negative numbers mean he is in the offense's backfield),
computed from their Big Data Bowl-format tracking frames exactly as you would from real data:

::: {#8dd1e518 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (depth past the line of scrimmage, from tracking frames)"}
def depth_table(plays, times=(0.3, 0.6, 1.0)):
    rows = []
    for name, play, key in plays:
        trk = play.to_tracking()
        los = trk.loc[(trk["displayName"] == "football") & (trk["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
        me = trk[trk["displayName"] == key].set_index("time")
        rows.append({"defender": name, **{f"+{t:.1f} s": round(float(me.loc[round(t, 1), "x"] - los), 1)
                                          for t in times}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("defender")


from IPython.display import Markdown


def as_markdown(df):
    """A small table as a Markdown pipe table (no index column), which prints cleanly in every format."""
    cols = list(df.columns)
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(cols) + " |", "|" + "|".join([":--"] + ["--:"] * (len(cols) - 1)) + "|"]
    rows += ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in r) + " |" for r in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    return Markdown("\n".join(rows))


as_markdown(depth_table([("one-gap 3-technique (simulated)", P_ONE, "R3"),
                         ("two-gap nose (simulated)", P_TWO_R, "NT")]).reset_index())
```

The same calculation on real frames is a few lines with `gridiron.bdb`. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season,
weeks 1–9) has every player's location ten times a second, and its players file has his position label, so you can find each interior
defensive lineman on each run and measure how deep he is at one second. Aggregated by player, it separates the
penetrators from the anchors, with two caveats. Position labels are rosters, not jobs: filtering on "DT" and
"NT" misses 3-4 ends who play a 4i or a 3 and edge players who slide inside on passing downs. And depth alone
can't tell a penetrator from a defender the offense *let* through: an unblocked man on a trap, an option read or
an influence block shows up deep in the backfield too. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this cell is not run
when the book is built.

::: {#c14a9759 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"}
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position", "displayName"]]
runs = plays[plays["isDropback"] == False]                       # not a dropback: designed runs (plus kneels)
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
if "position" not in trk:                                        # 2025 tracking has no position column:
    trk = trk.merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId", how="left")   # take it from players.csv

out = []
for g, pl in runs[["gameId", "playId"]].itertuples(index=False):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl, label="position")
    los = one.loc[(one["side"] == "ball") & (one["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
    at1 = one[(one["time"].round(1) == 1.0) & one["position"].isin(["DT", "NT"])]
    out += [{"nflId": r.nflId, "depth": r.x - los} for r in at1.itertuples()]

depth = (pd.DataFrame(out).merge(players, on="nflId")
         .groupby("displayName")["depth"].agg(["mean", "count"]).query("count >= 50").sort_values("mean"))
depth.head(10)    # the deepest penetrators (most negative = furthest into the backfield)
```
